summary: You implemented a correct brute-force pair search and avoided the common “reuse the same element” bug by starting j at i+1. However, the solution failed an edge test because it raised an exception on empty/no-solution input instead of returning an empty list, and it stayed at O(n^2) despite the problem’s scale (up to 1e5) where the expected approach is O(n) with a hash map.

thinking_and_logic: You followed a baseline-first approach: iterate all pairs (i, j) with j > i and return the first matching pair of indices. That reasoning correctly enforces distinct indices and will find the unique answer when one exists. The main gap was treating “no solution / empty” as impossible and encoding that assumption via an exception, which conflicted with the test contract, plus not upgrading to the hash-map approach needed for large n.
code_assessment: Your final code matches the answer key’s brute_force approach (nested loops) and therefore has O(n^2) time. The canonical optimal solution you missed is the single-pass hash map (value -> index) technique: for each number x at index i, check whether target-x has been seen; if so return [seen[target-x], i]; otherwise store x. That achieves O(n) time and is the expected approach for n up to 1e5. Separately, your function raises ValueError when it doesn’t find a pair; the tests expected [] for empty input, so the behavior should be adjusted to return an empty list (or otherwise follow the specified interface).
